                                                                                                       ENG516..…….
                                                     Lecture: 23

Variety of channels in businesses

       Letters
       Memos
       Emails
       Text messages

Rationale behind choosing one channel

       Topic
       Format
       Audience
       Security
       Destination

Purposes to write a letter

       Inquiries
       Cover letters
       Complaints
       Conveying bad news
       Confirmation
       Recommendations

Components of Letters

       The paper should be ‘8.5’ by ‘11’ with ‘1’ to ‘1.5’ margin on all sides
       Writer’s address or the company’s address
       The reader’s address should be placed two spaces below the date
       Salutation starts with ‘dear’ with your reader’s last name followed by a colon. If marital status of a woman is
        unknown ‘Ms’ should be used, and if known then ‘Miss’ or ‘Mrs.’.
       Letter body starts two places below the salutation and includes your introductory paragraph, the discussion
        paragraph(s) and the concluding paragraph.
       Complimentary close is placed two spaces below the letter body and includes, “Sincerely”

Types of Letters

Cover letter - you have to specify why and what you are writing about in the introduction, and if the information was
requested.

Letter of inquiry - written to give information about degree, requirements, costs, deadlines.

Transmittal letter - gives information to clients, vendors and tells upfront what they are receiving, helping to focus
readers’ attention on important things.

Recommendation letter - written to recommend an employee, a project or a service. Perhaps an employee deserves a
promotion or has to be nominated for an award.

Bad news letter – also starts with an introduction which is a buffer. It avoids telling why you are writing. In discussion
after giving the bad news, quantifiable evidence is given as background to the situation. The conclusion gives future
hope.

                                                                                                                2
                                                                                                       ENG516..…….
Formats of Letters

       Full Block - all the information is to the left side of the paper without indenting of paragraphs. The date and the
        complimentary close/ signature are also flush with the left margin.
       Full block with subject line - the only difference is that a subject-line is included.
       Simplified - The Simplified format omits the salutation and complimentary close e.g. sincerely

Considerations regarding writing a letter

   1) Steps of process writing
       Pre-writing
       Writing
       Re-writing
   2) Writing rules
       Clarity
       Conciseness
       Authenticity
       Ethics

                                                     Lecture: 24

Mostly used forms of communication

   1. Memos
   2. Emails
   3. Letters

The choice of channel (given above) depends on:

       The purpose of the communication
       The audience
       The security
       Accessibility

Writing criteria for memos

   1.   Identification line - summarizes the memo’s content and gives the date, to, from, subject
   2.   Introduction - why and what you are writing
   3.   Discussion - the content is developed specifically
   4.   Conclusion - the writer thanks the reader and adds a directive close

Criteria for memos

       Subject line
       Discussion
       Audience Recognition
       Style and Tone
       Format

Reasons for Writing Memos

       Can access those are working in the field
       Not all companies have access to email
       Some unions demand hard copies
       Some information cannot be sent electronically, e.g. cancelled checks

                                                                                                                3
                                                                                                       ENG516..…….
Business functions best conveyed through memos

          Status
          Directive
          Procedures
          Inquiry
          Documentation
          Confirmation
          Recommendations

Reasons for Writing Emails

Same as memo’s functions given above

                                                      Lecture: 25

Reports can differ according to:

          Purposes
          Length
          Formality
          Audience
          Channels

Functions of Report writing

          Informational: Give factual information
          Analytical: Analyze causes behind the information
          Persuasive: Give information and draw conclusions

Channels in which reports can be written

     1. Memos
     2. Emails
     3. Letters

Organization of a report

        Identification lines - consists of a date, to whom, by whom and a Subject. It has to have a topic and a focus
        Headings and talking headings – headings make text accessible and talking headings explain the headings
        Introduction - provides an overview of the report
        Discussion - discussion is the largest part of the report & includes development of concepts of summarized topics
        Conclusion/Recommendations - sum up the report and relate what decisions have been made, suggest actions

Types of Reports

          Incident report documents an unexpected happening, e.g. equipment failure, accident, employee misconduct
          Investigation report looks at the causes behind an incident. It is a document about why something happened
          Progress report gives the status of an activity, accomplished and remaining

                           (2025_Repeated Questions)
Q. What are the three types of communication?

Communication can be classified into three main types: verbal communication, non-verbal
communication, and written communication. Each type plays a crucial role in different contexts,
such as business, education, and social interactions.

Q. How are multicultural communication challenges addressed?

Multicultural communication challenges are addressed by acknowledging diversity, avoiding
ethnocentrism, defining terms clearly for diverse audiences, and being sensitive to cultural norms
regarding language, colors, humor, and symbols.

Q. How can cultural biases, humor, puns, and symbols (e.g., colors, animals) be managed in
multicultural communication?

These elements must be used cautiously as their meanings vary across cultures. For example,
certain colors like red and black can have both positive and negative connotations in different
cultures. Similarly, animals such as eagles or dogs may carry different symbolic meanings.
Humor and puns should be carefully considered to avoid misunderstandings.

Q. How do turn-taking and pausing show respect in different cultures?

In some cultures, turn-taking is structured and interruptions are considered rude, while in others,
overlapping speech is a sign of engagement. Similarly, pausing in conversation is viewed as a
natural part of dialogue in some cultures but may be perceived as awkward silence in others.

Q. What is e-learning? How is it effective?

E-learning refers to learning conducted via electronic media, typically on the internet. It is
effective because it allows for flexibility, accessibility, and personalized learning experiences
while incorporating multimedia elements for enhanced engagement.

Q. What are three advantages of e-learning?

   ❖       Flexibility, allowing learners to access content at their convenience.
   ❖       Interactivity, making learning more engaging through multimedia tools.
   ❖       Cost-effectiveness, reducing expenses related to traditional classroom-based learning.

Q. What is task-based assessment? Explain.

Task-based assessment evaluates a learner's ability to use language in real-world tasks rather
than through traditional tests. It focuses on practical communication and language use in
authentic situations.

Q. What is the role of intercultural training in education?

Intercultural training helps learners interact effectively with people from different cultures. It
enhances cultural awareness, communication skills, and adaptability, ensuring respectful and
effective cross-cultural interactions.

Q. What is the IMRD model in academic writing?

IMRD stands for Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion, a common structure used in
research papers and reports to present findings in a logical sequence.

Q. What is distance education?

Distance education is a learning system where students and instructors are separated by
geography or time and use technology such as online platforms, video conferencing, and digital
materials to facilitate learning.

Q. What are the benefits of distance education?

   ❖       Flexible learning schedules
   ❖       Access to a wide range of courses
   ❖       Reduced transportation and accommodation costs
   ❖       Opportunity for self-paced learning
   ❖       Enables learning from remote locations.

Q. What are five disadvantages of distance education?

   ❖       Lack of face-to-face interaction
   ❖       Technical difficulties
   ❖       Requires self-discipline and motivation
   ❖       Limited hands-on experience
   ❖       Risk of lower engagement and retention rates.

What is a web quest?

A web quest is an inquiry-based learning activity where students use online resources to explore
a topic, solve problems, or complete a project.

Q. What is the full form of CAT and CBT?

   ❖       CAT: Computer Adaptive Testing
   ❖       CBT: Computer-Based Testing.

﻿Lecture: 23
Variety of channels in businesses
    • Letters
    • Memos
    • Emails
    • Text messages
Rationale behind choosing one channel
    • Topic
    • Format
    • Audience
    • Security
    • Destination
Purposes to write a letter
    • Inquiries
    • Cover letters
    • Complaints
    • Conveying bad news
    • Confirmation
    • Recommendations
Components of Letters
    • The paper should be ‘8.5’ by ‘11’ with ‘1’ to ‘1.5’ margin on all sides
    • Writer’s address or the company’s address
    • The reader’s address should be placed two spaces below the date
    • Salutation starts with ‘dear’ with your reader’s last name followed by a colon. If marital status of a woman is unknown ‘Ms’ should be used, and if known then ‘Miss’ or ‘Mrs.’.
    • Letter body starts two places below the salutation and includes your introductory paragraph, the discussion paragraph(s) and the concluding paragraph.
    • Complimentary close is placed two spaces below the letter body and includes, “Sincerely”
Types of Letters
Cover letter - you have to specify why and what you are writing about in the introduction, and if the information was requested.
Letter of inquiry - written to give information about degree, requirements, costs, deadlines.
Transmittal letter - gives information to clients, vendors and tells upfront what they are receiving, helping to focus readers’ attention on important things.
Recommendation letter - written to recommend an employee, a project or a service. Perhaps an employee deserves a promotion or has to be nominated for an award.
Bad news letter – also starts with an introduction which is a buffer. It avoids telling why you are writing. In discussion after giving the bad news, quantifiable evidence is given as background to the situation. The conclusion gives future hope.

Formats of Letters
    • Full Block - all the information is to the left side of the paper without indenting of paragraphs. The date and the complimentary close/ signature are also flush with the left margin.
    • Full block with subject line - the only difference is that a subject-line is included.
    • Simplified - The Simplified format omits the salutation and complimentary close e.g. sincerely
Considerations regarding writing a letter
    1) Steps of process writing
    • Pre-writing
    • Writing
    • Re-writing
    2) Writing rules
    • Clarity
    • Conciseness
    • Authenticity
    • Ethics
Lecture: 24
Mostly used forms of communication
    1. Memos
    2. Emails
    3. Letters
The choice of channel (given above) depends on:
    • The purpose of the communication
    • The audience
    • The security
    • Accessibility
Writing criteria for memos
    1. Identification line - summarizes the memo’s content and gives the date, to, from, subject
    2. Introduction - why and what you are writing
    3. Discussion - the content is developed specifically
    4. Conclusion - the writer thanks the reader and adds a directive close
Criteria for memos
    • Subject line
    • Discussion
    • Audience Recognition
    • Style and Tone
    • Format
Reasons for Writing Memos
    • Can access those are working in the field
    • Not all companies have access to email
    • Some unions demand hard copies
    • Some information cannot be sent electronically, e.g. cancelled checks
Business functions best conveyed through memos
    • Status
    • Directive
    • Procedures
    • Inquiry
    • Documentation
    • Confirmation
    • Recommendations
Reasons for Writing Emails
Same as memo’s functions given above
Lecture: 25
Reports can differ according to:
    • Purposes
    • Length
    • Formality
    • Audience
    • Channels
Functions of Report writing
    • Informational: Give factual information
    • Analytical: Analyze causes behind the information
    • Persuasive: Give information and draw conclusions
Channels in which reports can be written
    1. Memos
    2. Emails
    3. Letters
Organization of a report
    • Identification lines - consists of a date, to whom, by whom and a Subject. It has to have a topic and a focus
    • Headings and talking headings – headings make text accessible and talking headings explain the headings
    • Introduction - provides an overview of the report
    • Discussion - discussion is the largest part of the report & includes development of concepts of summarized topics
    • Conclusion/Recommendations - sum up the report and relate what decisions have been made, suggest actions
Types of Reports
    • Incident report documents an unexpected happening, e.g. equipment failure, accident, employee misconduct
    • Investigation report looks at the causes behind an incident. It is a document about why something happened
    • Progress report gives the status of an activity, accomplished and remaining
Lecture: 26

Components of Resumes
    • Identification
    • Career Objectives
    • Summary of Qualifications
    • Employment
    • Education
    • Professional Skills
    • Professional Affiliations
    • Military Experience
    • Optional Components
    • Portfolios
    • References
    • Personal Data
Chronological resume
You write a reverse chronological resume if you are a traditional job seeker, a recent high school or college graduate, aged 18-25, and you hope to enter the profession in which you have received your college training or certification. In the resume you list your education and experience in reverse chronological order.
Functional resume
You write a functional resume when you are a non-traditional job applicant, returning to work after a gap and are not fresh graduate. You have not received education for a job and have changed jobs.
Ethical Considerations in CV
Your CV should give accurate information about your education, experience, skills and references. Inaccurate information can be found out, people can easily be contacted and checked.

In the business world, having strong linguistic skills is important for clear communication.

Effective communication goes beyond just knowing the language; it involves understanding how
to interact in different contexts and adapting to diverse situations.
For example, in negotiations, being able to navigate complex discussions and understand subtle
cues is crucial. Discourse competence allows individuals to tailor their communication styles to
different stakeholders, which fosters successful collaborations. This is especially important in
international business deals where cultural nuances play a pivotal role. Discourse competence
enables adaptability, increasing the chances of achieving a favorable outcome.
Additionally, presentations require more than just linguistic precision. A welldelivered
presentation involves gauging audience reactions, handling questions skillfully, and conveying
information persuasively. Discourse competence ensures seamless interaction and engagement
with the audience.
In summary, while linguistic competence is important, discourse competence serves as the bridge
that connects individuals and ideas in the dynamic business world. It empowers professionals to
navigate various scenarios, fostering effective communication and ultimately contributing to
success.

ENG516_Glossary

1. Accuracy :Accuracy in technical communication refers to grammatical and
   contextual correctness.
2. Achievable objectives :Achievable objectives are those objectives which are
   achievable and attainable in terms of abilities, realistic facilities and logistics.
3. Assessment and Evaluation :Assessment is concerned with individual student’s
   learning. Evaluation refers to course evaluation as a whole.
4. Authentic Materials :The term ‘authentic’ denotes that the texts were written
   for purposes other than language teaching and learning. Authentic materials
   could be real commercial documents, newspaper articles, recordings of meetings
   and conversations used in the workplace, newspaper clippings, excerpts from
   case studies, reports.
5. Aviation English :Aviation English is the de facto language of civil aviation
   which is called Radiotelephony; it is a specialized communication between pilots
   and air traffic controllers, and other personnel associated with the aviation
   industry.
6. Backwash Effect :When the course is designed with the test in mind, its effect
   is called wash back. Wash-back, according to Brown and Hudson, is “the effect
   of testing and assessment on the language teaching curriculum that is related to
   it”.
7. Business Communication :The communication which takes place at the
   workplace, in the educational setting, corporate office, or in a government job, is
   called business communication and is basically carried out in the English
   language.

By ASFAND YARR

                             ENG516_Glossary

8. Business English for Academic Purposes :English for academic purposes or
   EAP comes under the umbrella of ESP, and is required for those who use
   language to perform academic tasks or for employment.
9. Case Studies :A case study is a description of a problem or decision faced by a
   company business. It describes a specific business problem and creates a jumping
   off point for analysis and discussion.
10. Code of conduct :Code of conduct is the rules which are observed in different
   fields of life including education and pedagogy.
11. Communication Needs :Communication needs are the communication
   channels - traditional like letters and reports and the telephone as well as modern
   like the internet, intranet, fax, and instant messages-which we use to
   communicate.
12. Communicative Language Teaching :Communicative language teaching
   (CLT), aims to develop learners’ ability to use language to communicate. CLT is
   not a precise term and can mean different things to different people.
13. Controlling :Setting standards, checking actual performance against
   standards, taking corrective action as needed
14. Course Books :Course books are the major source of framework material
   which can be used extensively.
15. Dealing with Professional Content :A contentious issue in teaching of
   Business Communication is the amount of professional content in the course
   design.
16. Designing a Course :Designing a business English course is a matter of
   making a series of decisions based on information gathered during a needs
   analysis about learners’ communication, business and pedagogical needs.

By ASFAND YARR

                             ENG516_Glossary

17. Discourse Competence :Discourse competence, on the other hand, deals with
   language in use, although it is important to note that the word discourse can be
   used in a variety of ways by language professionals.
18. EAL :English as an Additional Language

   for purposes other than language teaching and learning. Authentic materials
   could be real commercial documents, newspaper articles, recordings of meetings
   and conversations used in the workplace, newspaper clippings, excerpts from
   case studies, reports.

   which is called Radiotelephony; it is a specialized communication between pilots
   and air traffic controllers, and other personnel associated with the aviation
   industry.

   is called wash back. Wash-back, according to Brown and Hudson, is “the effect
   of testing and assessment on the language teaching curriculum that is related to
   it”.

   workplace, in the educational setting, corporate office, or in a government job, is

   language.

ENG516 (Notes for {Grand Quiz})

                               10.Selection and Developing Materials
    Two types of materials can be used raw materials or authentic, e.g. newspapers, reports and
     published materials, e.g. course-books.
    When using published materials, if they are part of a unit, then activities can be created according
     to learners' needs.
    Raw materials are challenging, need effort to check suitability to be usable for the class.
     Adaptation and customization is needed.
    In designing tasks, especially for lower level students, attention to language level’ is required so
     as not to ‘turn off’ the students.
    The teacher has to balance suitability of raw and published materials in terms of:
         Relevance to learners’ objectives Quality of materials as learning tools The time needs
         for customization and adaptation Cost
    Features of Materials - suitability remains criteria
    In grammatical syllabus, its linguistic units and choose materials for it.
    A Business English syllabus can be based on:
         Identification of the elements that constitute the scope of Business English Selection of
         materials that fit the syllabus template
    Another approach sees classroom activities as the basis of material selection.
    The medium of materials could be: print materials - newspapers, reports, audio/video materials
     and multi medium materials.
    Equipment: The medium of materials could be audio which satisfies the above criteria, offers a
     wide range of choice in Business English courses and is cheap.
    Videos are also catching up with audio in popularity as they combine sound and picture, however
     are considered expensive ELT materials.
    The personal computer has revolutionized the way work is done.
    The telephone line has traditionally been used for distance learning.
    Video conferencing, email for feedback, Internet offers unlimited sources of topical and authentic
     material.
    The teacher has to balance suitability of these for particular learning aims.
    The most common ready-made material is course books, which are popular all over the world.
    Course books are textbooks, of which the teacher and the students have copies, which are to be
     followed systematically as the basis for course design.
    Disadvantages are that course books can get outdated easily.
    Important factors for learners could include learners’ specific requirements: Clear layout and
     structure, relevance, regular progress checks, revision opportunities, entertainment, self-study
     sections, reference sections, up-to-date content, and authenticity. Price can also be a factor.
    Teachers’ priorities could be the amount of guidance provided in a particular book, the extra
     activities, flexibility and ease of use.
    Publishers’ priorities are to satisfy teachers and students and catering for the needs of a wide
     clientele.
    Innovative teachers might feel using a course book is too conservative to go with new
     methodologies.
    Companies might not want too daring approaches and will prefer safe, traditional methods.
    A key issue when considering the choice of course book (or indeed any materials) is authenticity.

Maha Malik’s Compilation                                                                          Page 1

                          ENG516 (Notes for {Grand Quiz})

    There are many advantages of using authentic materials – it brings the real world into the class
     and provides motivation to learners by making the task realistic and useful for their future
     workplace.
    Authenticity could be of content and activities.
    Authenticity of activities is related to professional work.
    Presentation or negotiation is the main criterion for business success.
    Sometimes institutions and teachers find it important to produce tailor-made material, designed to
     supplement the course book or the regular course.
    This could be done by the training department or the individual teacher.
    Experienced teachers can have a huge amount of material which they can adapt to suit learning
     needs/contexts.
    Some of this adaptation can be merely cosmetic to make it look custom-made.
    Material used for an in-company course for a group of engineers in a multinational electrical
     engineering company based in France, of the production department.
    A KD router (a piece of electrical equipment) is a best-selling product can be used a group of
     property consultants based in Rome.
    Vocabulary, dates and place names can be adapted for learners of two different contexts.
    Generating Materials: Even if the teacher can get hold of genuine documents, the chances are
     they will need adapting, either because they may not be at an appropriate level, or they may only
     contain one or two ‘usable’ items, or because they are only relevant to a few people in the class.
    Ploughing through an irrelevant document can be extremely tedious, and may alienate learners.
    Materials are sometimes are so context-specific that they cannot be reused.
    Preparatory Stage: Material adaptation at this stage has to focus on:
        Assessment of the learners’ needs Deciding on priorities          Identifying and analyzing
     language items        Working out pedagogical approaches        Deciding what sorts of activities to
     use      Making decisions about layout        Evaluating or piloting early or draft versions
    Corpora (collections of real language data) can be an important source of material.
    It is authentic, as it is drawn from real language in use.
    A concordance is a list of phrases, each showing the same word or language feature taken from a
     corpus, which allows users to focus on a particular lexical, grammatical, or discourse issue

ENG516
What is Business Communication?

Business communication refers to the exchange of information within a business environment
and between an organization and its external stakeholders. It encompasses various forms of
communication, including verbal, written, and non-verbal, aimed at achieving organizational
goals. Effective business communication ensures clarity, efficiency, and collaboration,
contributing to the success of projects, negotiations, and customer relations.

Origin of Business Communication

The origin of business communication can be traced back to ancient trade practices, where
merchants used written records and verbal agreements to exchange goods and services. Over
time, the industrial revolution and globalization brought about formalized communication
channels, such as letters, memos, and telegraphs. With technological advancements, digital tools
like emails, video conferencing, and social media now dominate business communication.

Scope of Business Communication

Business communication has a broad scope, encompassing internal communication (e.g., team
meetings, reports) and external communication (e.g., marketing, client negotiations). It includes
corporate communication strategies like public relations, crisis management, and employee
engagement. The scope also extends to cross-cultural communication, addressing the challenges
of operating in global markets.

Development of Business Communication

The development of business communication aligns with changes in organizational structures
and technological innovations. Modern businesses emphasize collaborative tools, such as project
management software and instant messaging platforms, to enhance real-time interaction.
Additionally, the focus on emotional intelligence and cultural sensitivity has shaped
communication strategies to foster inclusivity and effectiveness.

Important Terms in Business Communication and ESP, EAP, EOP, EMP, ERPP

   •   ESP (English for Specific Purposes): Language tailored for specialized contexts like
       business, law, or healthcare.
   •   EAP (English for Academic Purposes): Focuses on academic skills like essay writing
       and research.
   •   EOP (English for Occupational Purposes): Language used in professional contexts,
       such as presentations and negotiations.
   •   EMP (English for Medical Purposes): Designed for healthcare professionals to
       communicate effectively in medical settings.
   •   ERPP (English for Research Publication Purposes): Helps researchers publish work in
       international journals.

Approach Not Product

This concept emphasizes focusing on the learning process rather than solely on outcomes. For
example, in teaching business communication, the emphasis should be on developing learners'
critical thinking and adaptability to communicate effectively in various scenarios, rather than just
mastering a fixed set of phrases or templates.

The Business English Learner

Business English learners often have diverse backgrounds and goals, such as improving
communication for meetings, writing professional emails, or participating in negotiations. These
learners may range from students preparing for careers in business to professionals seeking to
enhance their language skills for specific roles.

The Teaching Context

The teaching context involves the environment where Business English is taught. It includes
corporate training programs, university courses, or online platforms. The context shapes the
curriculum, materials, and teaching methods, considering factors like learners’ proficiency
levels, workplace demands, and cultural settings.

The Business English Teacher

A Business English teacher must possess a combination of linguistic expertise, business
knowledge, and adaptability. They should understand industry-specific terminology, cultural

nuances, and effective teaching strategies to meet learners’ diverse needs. The ability to design
customized lessons based on real-world scenarios is crucial.

Language in Context

Teaching Business English involves using language in context to make it relevant and applicable.
For instance, learners practice writing emails, participating in meetings, or preparing reports that
reflect actual workplace situations. This contextualized approach enhances retention and
practical application.

Teaching Business English

Teaching Business English focuses on improving learners’ communication skills for professional
settings. It involves integrating grammar, vocabulary, and pragmatic skills tailored to business
contexts. Methods include role-playing, case studies, and simulations to mimic real-world tasks
like negotiations or presentations.

Rationale of the Course

The rationale of a Business English course is to equip learners with the linguistic and
communicative skills necessary to excel in professional environments. It addresses specific
goals, such as improving fluency in workplace interactions, enhancing written communication,
and developing cross-cultural competencies.

Teaching Business Communication

Teaching business communication goes beyond language instruction to include interpersonal
skills like persuasion, clarity, and negotiation. Lessons focus on practical applications, such as
report writing, delivering presentations, and managing conflicts, using interactive methods to
build confidence and effectiveness.

Linguistic Competence

Linguistic competence refers to the ability to use correct grammar, syntax, and vocabulary in
communication. In business contexts, this involves mastering formal expressions, technical
terms, and appropriate tone to convey professionalism.

Discourse Competence

Discourse competence involves organizing language into coherent and meaningful texts or
conversations. Business communication requires structuring reports, emails, and presentations
logically, ensuring clarity and persuasiveness in professional interactions.

Q. Briefly describe the two components of Business English course.
The two components of a Business English course are language knowledge which reflect the formal aspects of grammar, vocabulary and sound system and communication skills in which we activate this knowledge to transmit messages through different channels, for example, oral channels like presentations, meetings, telephoning or in written documents such as letters and reports.
Q. Briefly describe the ‘stage three’ of practice of presentation.
Practice Stage 3: Each participant presents a transparency, for 2 to 3 minutes, practicing appropriate language and appropriate techniques, followed by discussion on delivery and techniques. Discussion is on the importance of strong and memorable ending.
Q.  Write a brief note on ‘mean analysis’. Your answer should not exceed four lines.
A means analysis is a description of the training environment - what is available in terms of equipment, facilities and time, and perhaps more importantly, what is not? Q. in which business English what is the first thing that make the English distinctive
(Topic_01)
The distinction between general and business English is not so clear. Although the objectives of
both are the same, that is, developing the accuracy, fluency and effectiveness of the target language
in the students; however, the context is different. In general English, one learns the basics, the
mechanics of grammar, composition and vocabulary. In business English you build upon what you
learned in general English, focusing on business situations, which require clarity, logic and
presentation styles that are dominant in business communication.
Q. Briefly describe the two components of Business English course. (Topic_01)
The two components of a Business English course are language knowledge which reflect the
formal aspects of grammar, vocabulary and sound system and communication skills in which we
activate this knowledge to transmit messages through different channels, for example, oral
channels like presentations, meetings, telephoning or in written documents such as letters and
reports.
Q. 2 dominant trends of WW. (Topic_02)
The importance of commerce and technology, which generated the demand for a unifying language
and because of various factors, one being the power of the USA, this role fell to English. As
English became the accepted international language, non-native workers and students needed it
for functional and academic purposes.
Q. Phase 1 of development business communication. (Topic_04)
The Concept of Special Language: Register Analysis. In 1960s and early 1970s, the basic principle
was that each field has its own particular register. Specific registers were to be analyzed to identify
their grammatical and lexical features to be used in teaching materials. The aim was to make the
syllabus as relevant as possible to learners’ needs, giving high priority to language forms that
students were likely to meet in Science studies. However, there was very little that was distinctive
in the sentence grammar of Science English, except a tendency to favor certain grammatical forms,
like the simple present tense, passive voice and nominal compounds. This meant that there was
nothing which was not present in General English (Ewer and Latorre 1969).
Q. Phase 2 developments in BC? (Topic_04)
Rhetorical or Discourse Analysis. In this phase, attention was given to language above the sentence
level, how sentences were combined in discourse to produce meaning. The aim was to identify
organizational patterns in texts, to specify the linguistic means by which these patterns were
signaled, and used to make the ESP syllabus.

Business communication teaching, like all ESP teaching, then is an approach to language teaching
in which all decisions as to content and method are based on the learner's reason for learning.

Corpora (collections of real language data) can be an important source of material. It is authentic, as it is

Internet). A typical concordance program can allow the user to isolate a particular language feature and

measurable objectives?

Measurable objectives measure whether objectives are met or not. They establish concrete
criteria for measuring progress toward the attainment of each objective you set. When you
measure your progress, you stay on track, reach your target dates, and experience the feeling of
achievement that drives you on to continued effort required to reach your objective. To determine
if your objective is measurable, ask questions such how much? How many? How will I know
when it is accomplished? If the objective is measurable, it means that the measurement source is
identified and we are able to track the actions as we progress towards the objective.

Measurement is the standard used for comparison. Measurements (and the visible progress) go a
long way to help us to know when we have achieved our objective.

Relevant objectives?

Relevant objectives in terms of leading to the desired results and relate to needs analysis, what is
their current communicative proficiency and what they should be at the end of the course. This
means two things; that the goal or target being set with the individual is something they can
actually impact upon or change and secondly it is also important to the organization, and is
relevant to what the organization is trying to achieve. The manager has to decide these objectives
by considering the wider picture.

Achievable objectives?

Achievable objectives see whether set objectives are achievable and attainable in terms of
abilities, realistic facilities and logistics. When you identify objectives that are most important to
you, you begin to figure out ways you can make them come true. The objective needs to be
attainable by you based on the skills you have and the constraints imposed.

Time-bound Objectives?

Time-bound Objectives are concerned with timely completion: When do you want to achieve
the set objectives? When will we accomplish/ complete this objective? In the objective
somewhere, there has to be a date (Day/Month/Year) for when the task has to be started (if it’s
ongoing) and/or completed (if it’s short term or project related). Time-bound means setting
deadlines for the achievement of the objective. Deadlines need to be both achievable and
realistic. If you don’t set a time, you will reduce the motivation and urgency required to execute
the tasks. Agreed time frames create the necessary urgency and prompts action.

specific objective?

A specific objective has a much greater chance of being accomplished than a general goal. To set
a specific objective you need to answer the six “W” questions: Who: Who is involved? What:
What do I want to accomplish? Where: Identify a location. When: Establish a time frame.
Which: Identify requirements and constraints. Why: Specific reasons, purpose or benefits of
accomplishing the goal. Instead of saying: “Awareness of …” it should be “Learners will be able
to speak about the ...” Rules of conciseness and correctness should be applied.

Objectives should be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound,
(SMART)to specify what they need to achieve, answering six questions: Who? What? Where?
When? Which? Why?

Explain Negotiating the Syllabus?

Negotiating the syllabus means involving learners in decisions about what should be learned and
how. It allows teachers to understand learners’ priorities, expectations, and preferences. The
process may include asking learners about their goals, preferred activities, or areas they want to
improve. This gives learners ownership and motivation and helps in tailoring the syllabus to
better meet their needs. By incorporating their views into the course design, the teacher can
create a more learner-centered and relevant syllabus.

Negotiation may occur at various stages—before the course begins, during the first lesson, or
even continuously throughout the course. Teachers may ask learners about:

   •   What topics they find most relevant

   •   What skills they want to improve (e.g., presentations, emails, telephoning)

   •   What formats they prefer (e.g., group work, one-to-one coaching)

The result is a syllabus that is co-created with the learners, which helps to increase motivation,
engagement, and effectiveness of learning. It also promotes autonomy, as learners take more
responsibility for their own development.

Many activities can be devised for negotiating the syllabus can be used on day one of a course,
for example the following: What the group wants - the teacher gives learners a sheet. They fill in
the first two questions on their own, and then pass the sheets round so that everyone can see what
their colleagues want and do not want and can understand that different people want different
things. The sheets are then used as a basis for the third question, the answer to which is, in effect,
the syllabus and which will have to be some amalgam of the differing priorities that have
surfaced. The learners come to know that what happens is actually a compromise. Getting them
to sign at the bottom of the page is a useful way to remind them that they are part of the success
of the course. These sheets can be used to review the course later:

   •   What I don’t want from this course • What the group wants from this course

   •   Date: .....................

   •   Signature: ...........................

Q. in which business English what is the first thing that make the English distinctive
(Topic_01)

The distinction between general and business English is not so clear. Although the objectives of
both are the same, that is, developing the accuracy, fluency and effectiveness of the target
language in the students; however, the context is different. In general English, one learns the
basics, the mechanics of grammar, composition and vocabulary. In business English you build
upon what you learned in general English, focusing on business situations, which require clarity,
logic and presentation styles that are dominant in business communication.

Q. Briefly describe the two components of Business English course. (Topic_01)

The two components of a Business English course are language knowledge which reflect the
formal aspects of grammar, vocabulary and sound system and communication skills in which we
activate this knowledge to transmit messages through different channels, for example, oral
channels like presentations, meetings, telephoning or in written documents such as letters and
reports.

Q. 2 dominant trends of WW. (Topic_02)

The importance of commerce and technology, which generated the demand for a unifying
language and because of various factors, one being the power of the USA, this role fell to
English. As English became the accepted international language, non-native workers and
students needed it for functional and academic purposes.

Q. Phase 1 of development business communication. (Topic_04)

The Concept of Special Language: Register Analysis. In 1960s and early 1970s, the basic
principle was that each field has its own particular register. Specific registers were to be analyzed
to identify their grammatical and lexical features to be used in teaching materials. The aim was
to make the syllabus as relevant as possible to learners’ needs, giving high priority to language
forms that students were likely to meet in Science studies. However, there was very little that
was distinctive in the sentence grammar of Science English, except a tendency to favor certain

Maha Malik’s Compilation                                                                      Page 3

                           ENG516 (Mids) Solved Fall2019

grammatical forms, like the simple present tense, passive voice and nominal compounds. This
meant that there was nothing which was not present in General English (Ewer and Latorre 1969).

Q. Phase 2 developments in BC? (Topic_04)

Rhetorical or Discourse Analysis. In this phase, attention was given to language above the
sentence level, how sentences were combined in discourse to produce meaning. The aim was to
identify organizational patterns in texts, to specify the linguistic means by which these patterns
were signaled, and used to make the ESP syllabus.

                                                                    ENG516..…….
These are notes for those students who are unable to go through video lectures &
handouts. These are not prepared for grand quiz but you can comprehend topics of
grand quiz or basic concepts.

                                                           Lecture: 01

Business Communication - The communication which takes place at the workplace, in the educational setting,
corporate office, or in a government job.
Business English - an umbrella term for a mixture of general everyday English, general Business English, and ESP.

Two components of a Business English course

    •        Language knowledge - reflect the formal aspects of grammar, vocabulary and sound system
    •        Communication skills - in which we activate this knowledge to transmit messages through different channels

General and Business English

    •        Objectives of both are the same
    •        Context is different
             ▪ In general English, one learns the basics, the mechanics of grammar, composition and vocabulary.
             ▪ In business English you build upon what you learned in general English

Impact of Revolution in Linguistics
This led to the awareness of the following:

         •     The differences between written and spoken language.
         •     The difference between the language of commerce and the language of engineering.
         •     The language needs of different groups are different.
         •     Also that if language varies from one situation of use to another, it should be possible to determine the
               features of specific situations and then make these the basis of learner's courses.

Areas of management

    1.       Planning
    2.       Leading
    3.       Organizing
    4.       Controlling

Communication has been influenced by a variety of disciplines

    •        Linguistics
    •        General language
    •        E - Learning
    •        Teaching and management training

ESP Phases of development

    1) The Concept of Special Language: Register Analysis. In 1960s and early 1970s, the basic principle was that
             each field has its own particular register.

                          Prepared by Mudassar Ahmad 2nd Batch                                                      2
                                                                                               ENG516..…….
    2) Rhetorical or Discourse Analysis. In this phase, attention was given to language above the sentence level,
        how sentences were combined in discourse to produce meaning.
    3) Target Situation Analysis/Needs Analysis. In this phase the aim was to take existing knowledge by
        analyzing the target situation and then identifying the linguistic features of that target situation.
    4) Skills and Strategies. In this phase, the attempt was to look below the surface to consider the thinking
        process that underlies the language use.
    5) Learner-centered Approaches: emphasized the leaner and his needs at the center of a course design.

ESP Tree
The tree represents some of the common divisions made in ELT. The top most branches show the level at which
individual ESP courses lie. So, we have:

    •   English for Medical Studies
    •   English for Psychology
    •   English for Technicians
    •   English for Economics
    •   English for teaching

The lower level shows the two common branches of ELT

    •   Whether the learner wants English for Academic Purposes (EAP)
    •   Or for Vocational Purposes (EVP) also called EOP or VESL

The next level down shows the three common branches of ELT

    •   EST (English for Science and Technology)
    •   EBE (English for Business and Economics)
    •   ESS (English for Social Sciences)

As we go down the tree, we see that ESP is just one branch of ESL and EFL, which are themselves the two main
branches of English Teaching in general.

Distinguishing between Business Communication and other forms of language teaching
The analogy of the tree has helped to show us what BC teaching is not:

    1) Business communication teaching is not a matter of teaching a ‘specialized variety’ of language.
    2) Business communication is not just a matter of business words for business students.
    3) BC teaching is not different in kind from any other form of language teaching.

BC; An approach or product

BC has to be seen as an approach not a product since business communication is not the teaching of a particular
language nor does it consist of a particular type of methodology or material. It should be taken as an approach to
language learning which is based on the learner's need.

                                                      Lecture: 02

People interact and communicate with each other all over the world for various purposes. Despite these differences, it
is possible to group together learners according to the following categories:

    1) According to Experience

                          Prepared by Mudassar Ahmad 2nd Batch                                                        3
                                                                                                      ENG516..…….

A Pre-experienced learner

    •   Learning to follow business career
    •   No experience of the business world
    •   Need teacher to understand business world

Job experienced
    • Experience of the business world
    • No need teacher to understand business world
    • Have precise ideas about what they need from a Business English course

General business-experienced
   • Falls between the two categories
   • Certain amount of job experience
   • Learning English to move into a new job

    2) Level in the Organization's Hierarchy: Learners at different levels in a company often have different
        approaches to business English learning.

    3) Target Situation Analysis/Needs Analysis. In this phase the aim was to take existing knowledge by
        analyzing the target situation and then identifying the linguistic features of that target situation.
    4) Skills and Strategies. In this phase, the attempt was to look below the surface to consider the thinking
        process that underlies the language use.
    5) Learner-centered Approaches: emphasized the leaner and his needs at the center of a course design.

ESP Tree
The tree represents some of the common divisions made in ELT. The top most branches show the level at which
individual ESP courses lie. So, we have:

    •   English for Medical Studies
    •   English for Psychology
    •   English for Technicians
    •   English for Economics
    •   English for teaching

The lower level shows the two common branches of ELT

    •   Whether the learner wants English for Academic Purposes (EAP)
    •   Or for Vocational Purposes (EVP) also called EOP or VESL

The next level down shows the three common branches of ELT

    •   EST (English for Science and Technology)
    •   EBE (English for Business and Economics)
    •   ESS (English for Social Sciences)

As we go down the tree, we see that ESP is just one branch of ESL and EFL, which are themselves the two main
branches of English Teaching in general.

Distinguishing between Business Communication and other forms of language teaching
The analogy of the tree has helped to show us what BC teaching is not:

    1) Business communication teaching is not a matter of teaching a ‘specialized variety’ of language.
    2) Business communication is not just a matter of business words for business students.
    3) BC teaching is not different in kind from any other form of language teaching.

BC; An approach or product

BC has to be seen as an approach not a product since business communication is not the teaching of a particular
language nor does it consist of a particular type of methodology or material. It should be taken as an approach to
language learning which is based on the learner's need.

    Lesson 01 ESSENTIALS OF BUSINESS ENGLISH AND BUSINESS COMMUNICATION

Topic– 001: What is Business Communication?

         The communication which takes place at the workplace, in the educational setting, corporate
office, or in a government job is called business communication and is basically carried out in the

      ENG516 Midterm Short Notes BY PIN2 and MUHAMMAD (MAS All Rounder)

      ENG516 Midterm Short Notes BY PIN2 and MUHAMMAD (MAS All Rounder)

English language. It is taught under various names - Business English and Business Communication or
Business Communication Workshop. We will be using the terms Business Communication and Business
English interchangeably during the course of these lectures.

        Communication takes an important place in the modern workplace. Business companies and
government departments have to carry out internal communication and external communication. The
globalized nature of modern businesses makes it imperative to communicate internationally with
multinationals and TNCs, for various purposes – like selling, persuading, negotiating, informing and
presenting. So a successful business today, depends for its success on individuals who are good and
effective communicators. The teaching of business English has therefore attracted increasing interest
and awareness in the last two or three decades. As the realization about its importance grows, business
English course books and other teaching and learning materials are proliferating and almost all the
undergraduates who study business, trade, finance, IT, commerce engineering, or medicine have to
take some courses in business English communication. The term Business English/Communication is
used to cover the English taught to a wide range of in-service, professional people, and pre-service
students in full-time educational programs preparing for a business career.

         Business communication has to be seen in the overall context of ESP. It is most definitely the
current growth area in ESP which, in the two or three decades, has attracted increasing interest and
awareness. Business English shares important elements with ESP - needs analysis, syllabus design,
course design, material selection and development etc. Business English or business communication is
a rapidly growing field within the area of English Language Teaching (ELT) and English for Specific
Purposes (ESP). Business English appeared as a course program on the ELT scene in the late 70s. It has
been shaped by ELT and non-ELT forces. Its course content and pedagogical practices combine English,
business and teachings, and it has received contributions from ELT methodologies, management
disciplines and communication studies.

         The two components of a Business English course are language knowledge which reflect the
formal aspects of grammar, vocabulary and sound system and communication skills in which we
activate this knowledge to transmit messages through different channels, for example, oral channels
like presentations, meetings, telephoning or in written documents such as letters and reports.
Language knowledge reflects what we know of language and communication skills means how to use
that knowledge.

        The distinction between general and business English is not so clear. Although the objectives of
both are the same, that is, developing the accuracy, fluency and effectiveness of the target language in
the students; however, the context is different. In general English, one learns the basics, the mechanics
of grammar, composition and vocabulary. In business English you build upon what you learned in
general English, focusing on business situations, which require clarity, logic and presentation styles that
are dominant in business communication. Business communication courses are also marked by
professional content, management skills and cultural awareness. It is generally thought that having
certain knowledge of general English is a prerequisite to start learning business English. This does not
mean that one needs to be fluent in English to start studying business English. There are business
English course books which are designed for different levels of knowledge of English learners. Business
communication courses do focus on language skills; however, this focus may take place in specific

      ENG516 Midterm Short Notes BY PIN2 and MUHAMMAD (MAS All Rounder)

        ENG516 Midterm Short Notes BY PIN2 and MUHAMMAD (MAS All Rounder)

teaching situations. Besides this, there is also a specific corpus, a particular context and a specific
communication. Therefore, its methodology also differentiates it from general English.

Topic - 002: Origin of Business Communication
       The teaching of business communication is not a coherent movement but grew out of the
converging of a number of trends, which are as follows:

a.      The post WW-II world has been dominated by two trends – the importance of commerce and
technology, which generated the demand for a unifying language and because of various factors, one
being the power of the USA, this role fell to English. As English became the accepted international
language, non-native workers and students needed it for functional and academic purposes.

b.      Oil crisis of 1970s resulted in a massive flow of funds and Western expertise into the oil-rich
countries. English language became a big business and commercial pressures began to exert their
influence, and demand on the English teaching profession for cost effective courses.

language was replaced by tailored courses which covered how language was used in actual
communication. Traditionally, the aim of linguistics was to describe the rules of English. However, new

1. Which of the following is a special meeting in which parties need each other’s agreement in
   order to achieve an effective result? (Negotiation)
2. Is it correct that ideally a role-play activity should give background information? (yes)
3. Is the following statement correct or incorrect? Negotiators are neither wholly distributive nor
   integrative. (correct)
4. Choose the correct option. Preparation of negotiation meeting includes ___________.
   (Assessing power)
5. Choose the correct option. Getting to know the other party in negotiation meeting is known as
   ___________. (Relationship building)
6. Is the following statement true or false? Identifying the key language for use in negotiations
   can be quite difficult? (true)
7. Is it true that the genre approach is an alternative approach to the teaching of writing? (yes)
8. Which of the following is the first step in the process approach to teach writing? (Prewriting)
9. Which of the following is about how sentences connect with each other to form a sense of
   unity? (Cohesion)
10.Is it true that the formatting allows the reader ease of access to the text? (yes)
11.In which of the following approaches learners are given the chance to study model texts and
   to base their own writing on what they have noticed in the texts? (Genre)
12.Is the following statement true or false? Determining the communication channel is an
   important feature of writing. (true)
13.Which of the following approaches to writing is a dynamic process? (Process)
14.Is the following statement correct or incorrect? Your choice of vocabulary, style and tone does
   not depend on who is going to read the report. (Incorrect)
15.Is the following statement correct or incorrect? Writing happens in a context; therefore, it has
   to relate to the setting. (Incorrect)
16.Is the following statement correct or incorrect? A Paired Crossword Approach combines the
   different threads of the course design. (correct)
17.Is the following statement correct or incorrect? Activities and practice of writing through
   controlled activities aim to develop competence in techniques, formats and language forms.
   (correct)
18.Letters are basically used for internal communication. (false)
19.One of the reasons for writing a letter is that Letters allow a better “paper trail” than emails
   and for a better documentation record. (true)
20.A letter should be ______ to have the desired effect on the recipient? (grammatically correct,
   All of the given, to the point and relevant, in the proper format)
21.At which place is a salutation used in a letter? (Opening)
22.Writing a letter provides more significance for correspondence. (correct)
23.The length of a letter can range from one page of text to more than three pages. (true)
24.A complimentary copy notation(cc) is used if a copy is being sent to other readers. (correct)

   people within a specific context. (Correct)

20.Choose the correct option. The simple throwaway line we might offer when we meet someone

Lesson 01
           ESSENTIALS OF BUSINESS ENGLISH AND
                     BUSINESS COMMUNICATION
Topic - 001: What is Business Communication?
What is the definition of Business Communication?
Business Communication is the communication that occurs in the workplace,
corporate offices, or educational settings and is primarily conducted in the
English language.
Why is effective business communication important in the modern workplace?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                         1

Effective business communication is crucial for success in the modern
workplace, as it involves both internal and external communication, often on a
global scale, for purposes such as selling, persuading, negotiating, informing,
and presenting.
How has the teaching of business English evolved in recent decades?
The teaching of business English has gained significance over the last few
decades, with a growing number of undergraduates from various fields needing
to take courses in business English communication.
What distinguishes business English from general English, and why is some
knowledge of general English necessary for learning business English?
Business English builds upon general English and focuses on business-specific
situations, emphasizing clarity, logic, and presentation styles. A basic knowledge
of general English is considered a prerequisite for learning business English.
Topic - 002: Origin of Business Communication
What are the key factors that contributed to the growth of business English
teaching?
The growth of business English teaching was influenced by the importance of
commerce and technology, the widespread use of English as an international
language, and the oil crisis of the 1970s, which led to a need for cost-effective
English language courses.
How did changes in linguistics impact the development of ESP and business
English?
Linguistics shifted from describing the formal aspects of language to focusing on
how language is used in real-life communication. This change emphasized the
differences between written and spoken language and the language needs of
specific groups.
How did developments in educational psychology influence the rise of ESP and
business English?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                               2

Educational psychology emphasized the importance of considering learners'
needs, interests, and motivation in language learning. This approach led to the
development of courses that catered to learners' specific requirements.
Topic - 003: Scope of Business Communication
What are the main components of a Business English course?
A Business English course typically consists of language knowledge (grammar,
vocabulary, and sound system) and communication skills (oral and written
communication in business contexts).
How does business English differ from general English in terms of context and
content?
Business English builds upon general English, focusing on business situations
that require clarity, logic, and specific presentation styles. It also includes
professional content, management skills, and cultural awareness.
What is the legitimate scope of business English teachers?
Business English teachers are responsible for designing and delivering courses
that aim to enhance language knowledge, communication skills, management
skills, cultural awareness, and the understanding of professional contexts.
Topic - 004: Development of Business Communication
What are the five main phases in the development of English for Specific
Purposes (ESP)?
The five main phases in the development of ESP are Register Analysis, Rhetorical
or Discourse Analysis, Target Situation Analysis/Needs Analysis, Skills and
Strategies, and Learner-centered Approaches.
How did these phases contribute to the development of ESP, including
business communication?
These phases contributed to ESP by shifting the focus from formal language
aspects to discourse, identifying organizational patterns in texts, analyzing
learner needs, exploring thinking processes underlying language use, and
emphasizing learner-centered approaches.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                             3

Topic - 005: Important Terms in Business Communication and ESP
What is the ESP tree, and how does it categorize various branches of English
language teaching?
The ESP tree categorizes various branches of English language teaching, such as
English for Science and Technology, English for Business and Economics, and
English for Social Sciences, under the umbrella of English for Specific Purposes
(ESP).
What are the distinctions between English for Academic Purposes (EAP) and
English for Vocational Purposes (EVP)?
EAP focuses on academic language needs, while EVP centers on language
requirements for vocational purposes, which include work-related and
professional contexts.
What are some specific terms related to business communication, such as
ESBP and EGBP?
ESBP stands for English for Specific Business Purpose, while EGBP stands for
English for General Business Purposes, targeting learners with limited working
experience.
Topic - 006: Approach not Product
What is Business Communication teaching considered, and why?
Business Communication teaching is considered an approach rather than a
product, as it emphasizes the learner's specific needs and is not a distinct form
of language.
What distinguishes Business Communication teaching from other forms of
language teaching?
Business Communication teaching is not different in kind from other language
teaching; it uses common language learning processes and methodologies. It is
distinguished by its focus on the learner's specific reasons for learning a foreign
language.
What is the primary driving force behind Business Communication teaching?

Topic - 031: Communication Needs
What is the purpose of a needs analysis in teaching a course?
The needs analysis is done to determine communication needs, business needs, and
pedagogical needs of learners and teachers before teaching a course.
How can different communication situations affect communication needs?
Different communication situations give rise to different communication needs,
and these needs can be traditional (like letters and reports) or modern (like internet,
intranet, fax, instant messages).
How is needs analysis conducted for learners' communication needs?
Needs analysis for learners' communication needs involves finding out what
learners need to do in English, such as using English with clients or writing
assignments.
What tools can be used for needs analysis in communication?
Tools for needs analysis include questionnaires, interviews, observation, and
commercially available tests.
Topic - 032: Main Priorities

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                               1

What is the purpose of a placement test in assessing communicative
competence?
A placement test assesses the current communicative competence of learners and
helps place them with others having similar needs and ability.
What are the characteristics of a reliable placement test?
A reliable placement test should be valid, have face validity, authenticity, and be
consistent in its results.
How do task-based assessments reflect real-life situations?
Task-based assessments use knowledge gained from the target needs analysis to
design tasks that reflect real-life situations, such as giving presentations for
business English learners.
Can you provide an explanation of how task-based assessments reflect real-
life situations and what steps are involved in designing such assessments?
Task-based assessments are designed to reflect real-life situations that learners will
encounter. For example, business English learners may be asked to give
presentations if they are expected to do so in their job roles. Designing these
assessments involves considering the target needs analysis and creating tasks that
mirror the actual workplace scenarios.
Topic - 033: Pedagogical Needs
What are pedagogical needs based on?
Pedagogical needs are based on the teacher's style, experience, and needs, the
learning environment, and the learning styles of learners.
What are some aspects of a teacher's role in addressing pedagogical needs?
A teacher's role can include being a trainer, coach, and consultant, adapting their
teaching style, and being a reflective practitioner.
Topic - 034: Language Styles
How can learning styles be influenced by culture?
Learning styles can be influenced by the culture of learners, where expectations of
the teacher's role may differ.
What is NLP, and how can it be useful to business English teachers?
NLP, or Neuro-Linguistic Programming, provides insights into communication
skills, including non-verbal communication, active listening, and perception, which
can be useful for business English teachers.
What is Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP), and how can it be applied in
teaching business English and enhancing communication skills?
Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP) is a collection of techniques and theories
that offer insights into how the mind works and how people communicate. NLP
can be applied to teaching business English by improving communication skills,
such as building rapport, non-verbal communication, and active listening, both for

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                             2

teachers and learners.
Topic - 035: Business Needs
Why is understanding business needs crucial for a BE teacher?
Understanding business needs is crucial because it helps the teacher align the
course with the sponsor's, company's, or department's expectations, ensuring that
the training is worthwhile.
What are some key aspects a teacher should consider about the company
when researching business needs?
The teacher should consider the company's product, market, size, and various
business functions, and understand the hierarchy of the company.
Topic - 036: Main Priorities
How does a practical needs analysis help in course design?
A practical needs analysis helps in course design by considering factors like target
situation analysis, communication needs, discourse, and means analysis, which
includes facilities and learner placement.
What role does the sponsor play in determining course design?
The sponsor often has a clear idea of the learners' needs and might influence course
design, as seen in formal reports and course design decisions.
Is needs analysis entirely objective?
Needs analysis is not entirely objective, as it involves decisions based on teachers'
interests, values, and beliefs about teaching, learning, and language. It is both
preparatory and ongoing.
